title: Pilate and Simon (Luke 23:13–26)
hookLine: a governor washes his hands; a passer-by from Cyrene is made to carry the cross
tomorrow: At the foot of the cross

lines: THE ONE WITH POWER, THE ONE PASSING BY.
cards: Some hard days have two kinds of people: the one with power to stop what's happening, and the one who happens to be walking by. One decides; the other can only help carry it. Jerusalem, in the morning.
After a night of questioning, Jesus is brought to the Roman governor, Pontius Pilate. Crucifixion is a Roman punishment, and the order will be his.
Outside the city, a man from North Africa is walking in from the countryside, with no idea what's coming.

teach.h: I FIND NO FAULT IN THIS MAN.
teach.b: Pilate questions Jesus and says to the chief priests and the crowd, in the King James Bible: "I find no fault in this man." In Luke he says it three times.
He sends Jesus to Herod Antipas, who mocks him and sends him back. Pilate offers to have him whipped and let go.
But the crowd shouts for Barabbas, in prison for rebellion and murder: "Crucify him, crucify him." And Pilate, who has the power, gives in. He releases Barabbas and hands Jesus over to be crucified.
The well-known hand-washing is in Matthew, not Luke: Pilate washes his hands before the crowd and says: "I am innocent of the blood of this just person: see ye to it."
But water doesn't wash away a decision. The order was Pilate's, and Roman soldiers carried it out.
For centuries some Christians wrongly blamed the Jewish people as a whole; the Catholic Church rejected that blame plainly at the Second Vatican Council, and other churches have too.

teach.h: SIMON OF CYRENE, FROM THE COUNTRY.
teach.b: Then Luke turns to Simon: "And as they led him away, they laid hold upon one Simon, a Cyrenian, coming out of the country, and on him they laid the cross, that he might bear it after Jesus."
Cyrene was in North Africa, in what is now Libya, and Acts mentions Jews from there in Jerusalem. Some readers think Simon was a pilgrim in town for the feast.

teach.h: THAT HE MIGHT BEAR IT AFTER JESUS.
teach.b: He didn't volunteer: Luke says they laid hold on him. But Mark names his sons, Alexander and Rufus, and some readers think the first audience knew them. If so, the man forced to carry the cross became part of the story.

how: Many Catholic, Anglican and Lutheran churches pray the Stations of the Cross in Lent, walking or meditating on fourteen moments of Jesus's last journey; Simon of Cyrene helping to carry the cross is the fifth. Christians often recite in the creeds that he suffered under Pontius Pilate.

a Roman soldier from the governor's guard

games.q: who said or did what — tap the pairs.
p: I find no fault in this man
washed his hands before the crowd

s: Luke tells the story of Pilate washing his hands
the hand-washing is in Matthew. in Luke, Pilate says three times he finds no fault.
Pilate gave the order, and Roman soldiers carried it out.
Simon of Cyrene volunteered to carry the cross
soldiers laid hold of him as he came in from the country and made him carry it.

games.q: you're Pilate. you've said three times you find no fault in this man. the crowd is shouting crucify him. what do you do?
o: release him, as you've said you'd do.
give in, release Barabbas, and hand Jesus over.
games.why: Pilate gives in. he releases Barabbas and hands Jesus over to be crucified. the power, and the decision, were his.

practice: Think of someone carrying something heavy right now: a diagnosis, a caregiving load, a lost job, a child in trouble, grief.

You can't take it away, and neither could Simon, but he could carry part of it for a while; picture one practical piece you could carry, a meal, a ride, an errand, a few hours of company. If you pray, you can hold them before God.

wordCard.voice: Cyrenian. A man from Cyrene in North Africa, pulled from the crowd and made to carry the cross after Jesus, on a morning Pilate had the power to stop and didn't.

orig.note: Greek: a stake or cross. The beam Simon of Cyrene was made to carry.
